assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty through the magic-wavelength idea, strontium and ytterbium lattice spectroscopy and extreme control of systematics. This is a measurement instrument that redefines what can be measured, and it already supports relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the planned redefinition of the second. It fits the view that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and led the first demonstrations. Ye's group drove the systematic-uncertainty reduction, the stability record and the link to frequency combs. The two-person configuration is clean and matches the supplied credit. Other lattice-clock groups (e.g. at NIST, PTB, SYRTE) and ion-clock work already recognised in 2012 and 2005 are not in the credited names, which leaves some peripheral credit questions.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have reproduced and surpassed 10^-17 to 10^-18 performance, and clock comparisons are routine. Timing is good. The redefinition of the second is still pending, but the work is mature and unusually well confirmed.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Exact allocation between Katori's conception and Ye's performance achievements; my knowledge of the detailed priority history is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and strain. It opened a large field with real applications in biology, materials and geophysics. The experimental demonstration of single-spin ODMR is the decisive step, followed by long coherence and quantum-sensing protocols.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko performed the first single NV optical detection and coherent control in 1997 and the following years. Lukin's group contributed nanoscale magnetometry proposals and demonstrations, quantum registers and sensing applications. Other groups (e.g. Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth) also made major contributions and are not in the credited list, so the three-person set is defensible but leaves overlooked contributors.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of independent confirmation by many groups and commercial sensor devices. Mature and timely. The application base keeps expanding.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across a large community; a three-person cut leaves out important experimental contributors.
Whether Lukin's contribution is best recognised here or in a Rydberg or quantum-network context.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, the superfluid to Mott transition, and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This turned quantum many-body theory into something that can be measured, with direct imaging of correlations. The impact on many-body physics is large, though the 2001 BEC prize and others cover parts of the underlying methods.
assessment.attribution: The credited set mixes theory (Cirac, Zoller) with experiment. As an experimentalist I would favour Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, who did the Mott insulator, fermionic Hubbard and microscope demonstrations. Greiner's microscope and the Jaksch-Zoller proposal ordering create a real allocation question, and the five-name credit exceeds a three-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups, the interpretation is stable, and quantum gas microscopes and fermionic Hubbard simulations are established. Still evolving toward questions like the doped Hubbard model and the pseudogap, so the ultimate headline result is not yet complete.
uncertainties: Allocation between proposal-side theorists and the experimentalists.
Whether recognition for a still-maturing simulation programme is premature compared with more finished results.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion quantum gate proposal and its experimental realisation underpin the leading digital quantum-computing and simulation platform, with record fidelities and growing commercial machines. The experimental coherence and gate fidelities are exactly the kind of demonstrated performance I value. Overlap with the 2012 Wineland prize on ion control is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal. Blatt led European experimental implementations, including entanglement of many ions and quantum simulation. Wineland's NIST work, already awarded, and Monroe's and Wineland's gate demonstrations complicate credit, and the credited names omit Monroe.
assessment.maturity: Platform is mature, replicated worldwide and has hardware roadmaps. The fundamentals are well confirmed. The risk is that 2012 already addressed ion control and that the scalable-computer story is not yet final.
uncertainties: Degree of overlap with the 2012 prize.
Omission of other experimental leaders such as Monroe; whether Blatt or Monroe is the better experimental choice is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provides strong coupling between superconducting artificial atoms and microwave photons and underlies the transmon and nearly all superconducting quantum processors. Experimentally clean demonstrations (Wallraff 2004) and a precise theory (Blais) have enabled a large field, including dispersive readout and quantum error-correction experiments.
assessment.attribution: Wallraff, Schoelkopf and Blais authored the decisive 2004 papers, with Girvin as a theory contributor. A three-person set of Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Blais is workable but excludes Girvin. The transmon contribution also belongs to Schoelkopf's group. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which is adjacent and may reduce appetite for another circuit-related prize soon.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and widely replicated, with large industrial uptake. Timing could be seen as slightly early after the 2025 prize.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 superconducting circuit prize.
Whether Girvin should replace Blais in the three-person set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry delivers precision measurements of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants and is a clear case of a new measurement technique opening new observations, including gravimetry for mineral exploration and navigation that I find convincing. Large-baseline tests of equivalence-principle and gravitational-wave detection concepts extend it.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's early interferometer with atoms and gratings, Bordé's theoretical and Ramsey-Bordé interferometry contributions, and Kasevich and Chu's atom interferometer gravimeters all carry priority claims. The credited list omits Chu and Chu's 1997 Nobel link, and four names are credited so a three-person choice drops one, which is unsatisfying.
assessment.maturity: The technique is well confirmed and commercial gravimeters exist. Performance headline results (e.g. fundamental tests) are still progressing, so timing is acceptable but not pressing.
uncertainties: Complex priority history among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu.
Whether the major scientific payoff is already realised or awaits future tests.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg tweezer arrays enable quantum simulation and increasingly computing with tens to hundreds of atoms, including recent error-corrected logical-qubit demonstrations. The experimental control of individual atoms is impressive, and the field is moving fast.
assessment.attribution: The decisive experiments came from Lukin and Greiner-Vuletic-linked groups, Browaeys and Grangier, and Saffman's gate proposals and demonstrations. Zoller's early theory is credited but I would pick the experimental trio. Many strong groups (e.g. Bernien, Ahn, Weiss) are outside the credited set.
assessment.maturity: Recent and rapidly evolving, so the final shape of the key contribution is not settled. A prize now would risk being premature relative to other more mature candidates.
uncertainties: Unclear separation among simulation, gates and error-correction contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Ti:sapphire laser and passive mode-locking made femtosecond pulses practical and reliable, enabling nonlinear microscopy, frequency combs and attosecond science. Its enabling impact is huge, though some downstream fields have already been recognised (frequency combs 2005, attosecond 2023, CPA 2018).
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire gain medium, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode locking, and Keller invented the semiconductor saturable absorber mirror. These are distinct contributions that fit three laureates, though Kerr-lens priority also involves others and the CPA prize overlaps in laser-technology spirit.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and widely used. Recognition is long overdue if anything, but the novelty relative to prior prizes weakens the case.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005, 2018 and 2023 laser-technology prizes.
Priority between Kerr-lens and SESAM routes.
